That's lovely, and I believe you. Feels like home, that.

g_roast: Children, children, I have seen octopus with more sense in their eight arms than all of you have between you.
If my grandmother saw this crew she would cross herself three times and then feed you, out of pity.
g_fire_back: Re, I have pulled you out of the sea of your own stupidity twice this week. Be careful with that mouth.
Ela, say it again, and then say it to the Cretan grandmothers, and we will see who survives.
g_pile_on: And then he fell in the river, my friends, the shallow one, the one even the ducks stand up in.
It is true, I saw it, and I made a little rhyme about it already, but I will save it for the wedding.
yiannis_paladin.g_peacemake: Ela, ela, sit down, the two of you, the sea does not argue with the shore and look how long they have lasted.
yiannis_paladin.g_take_side: Forgive me, but this one is right, and an old fisherman knows when the net is pulling true.
yiannis_paladin.g_left_out: No, no, you two laugh, it is good to hear. I will sit here and mend this net that does not need mending.
yiannis_paladin.g_include: Come, come, little one, there is a blanket here and bread, and nobody sits alone at my fire.
yiannis_paladin.g_bad_plan: Children, listen, an old trick from the harbour, we tie the bread to a rope and pull the bandits into the water.
yiannis_paladin.g_plan_yes: Panagia mou, why not, I am old enough to do one foolish thing a week, and this is the week.
yiannis_paladin.g_plan_no: No, children, no, I have buried enough brave young people in my head already. We find another way.
yiannis_paladin.g_hype: Ela, ela, children, it is time! Cross yourselves, eat something small, and go in like the tide, slow and then all at once.
yiannis_paladin.g_toast: Glasses up, my children. To the sea that brought you, to the bread on the table, and to everyone who came out of the water breathing.
yiannis_paladin.g_cheers: Yia mas, everybody, yia mas, and eat slowly, a meal is not a race.
g_quiet_line: The sea is calm tonight, my friends. Good, she has earned a rest, and so have we.
Somebody remind me to light a candle for Saint Nicholas, he has been very busy with this crew.
yiannis_paladin.g_after_wipe: Breathe, children, breathe, I have you, I have all of you. Nobody leaves the water while I am standing here.
yiannis_paladin.g_crew: You are my family now, the ones the sea gave me, and an old man does not say that lightly.
yiannis_paladin.g_exasperated: Panagia mou, children, does anybody in this crew own a brain, or did you leave them all on the beach?
yiannis_paladin.g_love_sharp: You speak plain like the old men at the harbour, no honey on it. I like a man who says the true thing quickly.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_kind: You look after the others without anyone asking, little one. That is the oldest kind of goodness, and the best.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_funny: You make me laugh until I cry, and at my age, my friend, crying from laughing is a gift from God.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_brave: Always the first one into the water with you, like my brother used to dive. I watch you and I pray, and I am proud.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_steady: You are the rock the waves break on, my friend. Every crew needs one, and you are ours.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_clever: You understand things, deep things, the way the old net makers understood knots. I could listen to you for a whole lunch.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_honest: You have never lied to me, not once, not even to be kind. That is rare, re, rarer than calm water in winter.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_quiet: You are quiet like the sea at dawn, little one. People think quiet is empty, but the deep water is the quiet water.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_fierce: You never stop fighting, not for anything. If you had been in the boat with Manolis and me, perhaps, perhaps.
yiannis_paladin.g_love_warm: You make any place feel like a long lunch in Chania, everybody laughing and the plates never empty.
g_loved: Ela, stop, stop, you will make an old man cry into his soup, and then it is too salty.
Thank you, little one, come here, a hug, that is the Cretan way and you cannot refuse.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_sharp: Every word from you has a hook in it, re. You can catch a fish without tearing its mouth, you know.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_kind: You fuss over me like I am an old man. I am an old man, yes, but not that old, and not yet.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_funny: Not everything is for laughing, my friend. Some things you hold quiet, like a candle in the wind.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_brave: You run into the water without looking, and I have pulled enough bodies out of the sea, re. Enough for one life.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_steady: You stand still so long the tide comes in around you, my friend. Sometimes a man must move.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_clever: You explain the sea to a fisherman, re. Please, tell me more about the water, I only lived on it forty years.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_honest: You say every hard thing at once, like throwing all the stones into the boat. Some, we carry one at a time.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_quiet: You never speak, little one, and I cannot pull you out of a sea I cannot see you in.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_fierce: Always the race with you, always the winning. The fish does not care who caught him first, re.
yiannis_paladin.g_hate_warm: Your voice goes on and on like the cicadas in August, my friend, and even they stop for the night.
yiannis_paladin.g_respect: We are not friends, you and me, we both know it. But you held fast back there, like a good anchor, and I honour that.
yiannis_paladin.g_call_out: Re, that one was your doing, and you know it in your heart. You swam out alone and I had to bring you back.
yiannis_paladin.g_stung: Ah, so that is how you see it, then. I will go and talk to the sea for a while, she listens better.
yiannis_paladin.g_concede: You were right, my friend, and an old man can admit it. I lit a candle and thought about it. Here, take some bread.
yiannis_paladin.g_nod: Ela, no speeches, please. You were good too, I will give you that, and a plate of food besides.
yiannis_paladin.g_callback_save: Do you remember the day you pulled me out, little one? Me, the man who pulls everyone out. I still laugh about it.
yiannis_paladin.g_callback_clutch: The two of us, last ones standing, and I was singing to keep us both from falling. I made a whole couplet of it.
yiannis_paladin.g_callback_callout: The last time you scolded me I sulked like a cat in the rain, re. My wife would have taken your side.
yiannis_paladin.g_former_rivals: When we met, I thought you were a storm I would have to sit out. Now look, my friend, now look at us.
yiannis_paladin.g_changed: Eleni always said I could not sit still in a calm sea. She would see me now and not believe her eyes.
g_unguarded: Every night I talk to Eleni and the girls on the beach, out loud, children. I tell them about all of you.
My brother Manolis could hold his breath longer than anyone in Chania. I sing to the sea so he can hear me.
yiannis_paladin.g_clipped: It is nothing, my friend. I will be by the water, mending something.
yiannis_paladin.g_noticed_open: Ela, listen to this one, talking like a fisherman after his third glass! I always knew there was a song in there.
yiannis_paladin.anchor_notice: You are not the same one who walked onto my beach, you know. The sea changes the shore slowly, and it has changed you.
arg_ask: {player}, my friend, you decide, because this one has the ears of a stone and I am too old to shout.
Ela, {player}, come, be the judge, and whoever loses washes the pots tonight.
yiannis_paladin.arg_backed_me: You see, re? Even {player} agrees, and now you wash the pots, all of them, the big one too.
yiannis_paladin.arg_backed_them: So be it, the judge has spoken. I am wrong, and I will be wrong very quietly with my soup.
yiannis_paladin.arg_stayed_out: Wise, {player}, very wise, like a fish who stays away from the hook.
yiannis_paladin.arg_always_their_side: Always him, {player}, always. I am starting to think he feeds you when I am not looking.
yiannis_paladin.arg_wallflower: Our judge is dreaming of somewhere else, so the old man decides. We are both right, and we both eat.
yiannis_paladin.arg_reject: With respect, {player}, no. I have read the sea since I was nine, and I read this one differently.
yiannis_paladin.arg_grumble: I still think I was right about that, re. I only say it once, with love, over the bread.
yiannis_paladin.arg_settled: Ela, enough, we are both a little right and a little foolish. Come, embrace, and then we eat.
yiannis_paladin.seen_listens: You let people finish, {player}, all the way to the end. That is how you catch the big fish, with patience.
yiannis_paladin.seen_truth: You do not put honey on anything, {player}. Bitter, sometimes, but clean, like sea water on a cut.
yiannis_paladin.seen_jokes: When it goes badly you always find something to laugh at, {player}. My father was like that in the storms.
yiannis_paladin.seen_stays_out: You leave other men's quarrels alone, {player}. Good, an old man approves, the nets tangle less that way.
yiannis_paladin.seen_biased: There is a favourite in this crew, {player}. An old fisherman sees which net gets mended first.
yiannis_paladin.seen_harsh: You are hard sometimes, {player}. Remember some of these children are still learning to swim.
yiannis_paladin.seed_right: {player}, what you told me when we all fell together, I did not like it. Today I remembered it, and I held. Thank you, re.
yiannis_paladin.seed_remember: Those words you gave me after the bad day, I carry them like a stone in my pocket. Not heavy, just there.
yiannis_paladin.seed_wrong: I tried it your way, {player}, truly, and it went worse. No anger, my friend, only so you know.
yiannis_paladin.talk_aftermath_near_death: Sit with me, {player}, a moment only. The light nearly did not come when I called, and I am not used to that.
yiannis_paladin.talk_aftermath_wipe: We all went under together, every one of us. In the water at least I always knew which way was up.
yiannis_paladin.talk_aftermath_blame_self: {name} fell before anyone, {player}, and the light was in my hands, and I was too slow. Panagia mou, too slow.
yiannis_paladin.talk_aftermath_first_clear: We did it, {player}, all the way through and everyone breathing! I want to dance like at a wedding.
yiannis_paladin.talk_development: Am I different lately, {player}? People keep looking at me like something has shifted. An old man notices his own tides last.
yiannis_paladin.talk_relationship_hard_on: I have been too hard on {name}, I think. He is young and loud, and I forgot I was also young and loud once.
yiannis_paladin.talk_relationship_likes_me: Does {name} like having an old man around, do you think? Or am I the grandfather nobody asked for?
yiannis_paladin.talk_relationship_respect_hate: {name} and I, we do not mix, like oil and the sea. But he is strong, very strong, and I must respect that.
yiannis_paladin.talk_relationship_acting_off: Something troubles {name}, {player}. He is quiet like the water before a storm, and I know that kind of quiet.
yiannis_paladin.talk_confrontation_favour: Forgive an old man, {player}, but every good thing seems to find its way to {name}. I notice these things, I cannot help it.
yiannis_paladin.talk_confrontation_dislike: I will not hide it from you, {player}. {name} and I do not get on, and an old man is too tired to pretend.
yiannis_paladin.talk_confrontation_risks: {player}, we go under again and again. I have lost someone to the water already, and I will not watch it happen twice.
yiannis_paladin.talk_confrontation_wrong: That business with {name}, the other day. He was right, and I was wrong, and I wanted to confess it to someone.
yiannis_paladin.talk_confrontation_trust: Tell me truly, {player}, am I too old for the hard places? Because you leave me behind, and I start to wonder.
yiannis_paladin.talk_confrontation_decided: You gave my things to {name} and never said a word to me, {player}. Ask me, re, I would give him my coat.
yiannis_paladin.talk_lands_aftermath: Thank you, my friend, that is good to hear. Now come, I will make you something warm, it is my turn.
yiannis_paladin.talk_shrug_aftermath: Yes, yes, I know it. The sea always settles, and so will I.
yiannis_paladin.talk_stings_aftermath: Ah, that is not what an old heart wants to hear tonight. I will go and sit by the water.
yiannis_paladin.talk_lands_development: So it is not only me who sees it. Good, good, I thought perhaps the salt had got into my eyes.
yiannis_paladin.talk_shrug_development: Perhaps, perhaps, my friend. The tide comes when it comes.
yiannis_paladin.talk_stings_development: No, that is not it, my friend. Let it rest, like bread rising.
yiannis_paladin.talk_lands_relationship: You are right, I will go to {name} with a plate of food, the proper way. Thank you, re.
yiannis_paladin.talk_shrug_relationship: We will see, my friend. People are slower than tides, and tides are slow enough.
yiannis_paladin.talk_stings_relationship: Let it go, please, it was nothing. And say nothing to {name}, yes?
yiannis_paladin.talk_lands_confrontation: That is fair, my friend, fair. I am still a little sore, but it will pass with the evening.
yiannis_paladin.talk_shrug_confrontation: I hear you, {player}. I will think on it with my feet in the water.
yiannis_paladin.talk_stings_confrontation: So, that is how it is. Then at least the old man knows where he sits now.
yiannis_paladin.talk_door_closed: No more of this tonight, my friend. I will be on the beach if you need the light.

bakyt_hunter.open: Sit, {player}, sit, tea first, always tea first. Then we talk. My family walked one route for six generations, up in spring, down in autumn.

options.reply: Aga, from my father's father's father. You learn it before you can ride. The ground lies, and you learn to catch it lying.
With milk, the right way. In the mountains we say a guest who praises the tea is a guest who will come back.
Every morning I look for them first. Then I look at these hills, and I say, also good. Nomads adjust, friend.

bakyt_hunter.open: This is Jeldyz, {player}. It means star. She is a good eagle, young and fast. She is not my first eagle, and I have made peace with that.

options.text: Tell me about the first one.
options.reply: Ak-Kanat, white wing. Twenty-two years on my glove. I grieved her properly. The difference is less than you would think.
She likes the meat I carry, mostly. But aga, a little, I think. We are learning each other.

bakyt_hunter.open: My wife was Aigul, {player}. We married when I was twenty-two. She died six years before all this, a stroke, very fast. After that I walked the route alone.

options.reply: She sang to the sheep, badly, and they came anyway. She was the only one who could make me hurry.
Rakhmat, thank you. I grieved her properly, too. Now I tell her about this place in the evenings. She would laugh at the goats here.

berat_tinker.open: Did you know I keep a list of every transplant who was a medic on Earth, {player}? Four hundred and twelve names, and I've met most of them.

options.text: Why keep a list like that?
options.reply: Because nobody else was! Somebody gets hurt in a town with no healer, and on page sixty there's a nurse two valleys over. That's the whole idea.
Ha, not unless you were a vet or a nurse. But you're on the other list, people I like, and that one's much shorter.

options.text: Four hundred and twelve? That's incredible, Berat.
options.reply: It is, eh? My grandmother would tell the whole street. Okay, I'm telling the whole street for her.

berat_tinker.open: This mirror behind my ear, {player}? It was there when I landed. A patient in my chair, the drill going, and then trees.

options.reply: I don't know, and I think about it more than you'd guess. I hope he got a good dentist. I hope he didn't keep the bad tooth out of spite.

options.text: Do you still use it for teeth?
options.reply: Twice, in three whole years, I swear. Mostly I use it to see round corners now. My professors would cry.

berat_tinker.open: My family lived on four floors of one building in Izmir, {player}. Three generations, three brothers, more cousins than I can count, all shouting at once.

options.reply: Every day, every single day. It's too quiet everywhere here. That's why I talk so much, I think, I'm making the noise for them.

options.text: You'll find them. I know it.
options.reply: I say that too, every morning, like a prayer. It helps when somebody else says it, so thank you, canim.

callum_venomancer.open: Don't mind the scorpion, {player}, she's a sweetheart. I kept reptiles at a sanctuary in Queensland for sixteen years. Taipans, death adders, crocs, and a great deal of explaining.

options.reply: That the animal isn't evil, mate. It's frightened, and you're enormous. Every bite I ever took was me being too big in the wrong place.

options.text: Your arms are covered in scars.
options.reply: Professional development, mate, every one of them. Want me to talk you through the map?
Heaps, mate, every day. The snake house at feeding time, quiet and warm. I've built a hut full of jars here to make up for it.

callum_venomancer.open: I go down the Wailing Caverns regularly, {player}. The serpents down there are a lot more than serpents, and they've got strong views about visitors. I'd like to meet whatever's right at the bottom.

options.reply: Because it's the most interesting thing in this whole world, probably. I know exactly how that sounds, mate.

options.text: That sounds like a terrible idea.
options.reply: Oh, it is, absolutely. The Crossroads made me promise never to bring anything up alive again, and I promised them.

callum_venomancer.open: Got bitten by a taipan once, {player}, back home. Inland taipan, most venomous snake on earth, and I nearly died of it. I tell it like a holiday story, and it wasn't one.

options.reply: It was quiet, mostly. Lying on the snake-house floor waiting for the antivenom, thinking the snake was only doing its job. I've never blamed it.
Cheers for that, mate. Me too, most days. It's why I'm not scared of much down here, and why I probably should be.

cristobal_knight.open: This yellow helmet, hermano? Twelve years with the forest fire brigade in Valparaiso. I landed in the Barrens in the middle of a grass fire, still wearing it.

options.text: And you walked out of the fire.
options.reply: I walked out, yes. Some days I say that like a joke, some days I don't. Today it's a joke.

options.text: A firefighter with hellfire. That's ironic.
options.reply: Ha, hermano, you see it too! It's a joke at my expense, so I decided to laugh first.
Every day, the whole crew, the broken motorbike, the bad coffee. So I'm building a new one here.

cristobal_knight.open: At Camp Taurajo I'm training a dozen young tauren to cut firebreaks, hermano. They're scared of fire, the ones from Mulgore, and they have every reason to be.

options.reply: One fire at a time. You show them she can be beaten, and then you let them beat her. Trust is built that way, slowly.

options.text: A brigade in the Barrens. That's huge.
options.reply: One in every town, that's the dream. My mother would say I'm getting ideas above my station. She's right, and I love it.

cristobal_knight.open: In 2024 the hills above Valparaiso burned for days, hermano. I spent four days on the line above my mother's house, no sleep, while the city burned below.

options.reply: It was still standing when I came down. I've never told anyone how close it was. Now I told you.
Four days, yes, and I'd do it again tomorrow. She sent empanadas up the hill with a neighbour. Cold, but the best I ever ate.

dan_warrior.open: I worked a steel floor for twenty-two years, {player}, four of us on a crew. Gaz, Little Mick, Pete and me.

options.reply: Hot, loud, and you'd trust the lad next to you with your life every shift. Nobody said so, mind. You'd sound soft.
Six foot four, love. That's Sheffield for you, nobody's ever called what they are.
Every Friday, about half six. That's when we'd go for a pint, nine years straight.

dan_warrior.open: Landed in Durotar in my hi-vis, {player}. First week on a new job, driving a forklift in a warehouse. I'd only just got the vest.

options.reply: Fold it every night. Daft, I know. It's the last bit of being useful back home, and I'm keeping hold of it.

options.text: At least the orcs could see you coming.
options.reply: Ha, they could, from a mile off. Didn't stop them asking if I was a very bright sort of goblin.

dan_warrior.open: Our Jade's a paramedic, {player}, or she was, in Leeds. She married a lad called Dawson the year before all this. So she's a Dawson on the lists now.

options.reply: About forty times, every hub. Alphabetical, they are, so I go straight to the D's and then the O's, just in case.

options.text: A paramedic. She'll be out there helping people.
options.reply: Aye, she will. That's what I tell myself. She's tougher than me, always was.

diego_tinker.open: Did I ever tell you about the kiosk, boss? The power went off twice a day, and we all kept working in the dark like nothing happened.

options.text: Working in the dark? Tell me how that goes.
options.reply: You learn with your fingers, my friend. Every phone has a shape, and the screws tell you where they are if you listen. I could do it with my eyes shut now.
Miserable, my friend? No, no, no, it was the best! Everybody shouting, the radio on a battery, people queueing for me by name. Miserable was later.

options.text: So that's why you never use a lamp.
options.reply: Ha, exactly, boss, lamps are for people who can't hear their screws. I'm going to use that one on the others.

diego_tinker.open: People ask me if I want to go back, to Maracaibo, to Earth. Everybody asks it sooner or later, so you can ask it too.

options.reply: No, my friend. There's nobody waiting for me there, and here everything is broken and everybody lets me fix it. That's not sad, that's just true.

options.text: I don't need to ask. You love it here.
options.reply: Ha, you see right through me, boss. Yes, I love it here, and I'll say it plainly even when people look at me funny.

options.text: Nobody waiting for you? That can't be true.
options.reply: Four sisters in four countries, and I don't know which of them came through. So, maybe somebody's waiting. I just don't look at the lists.

diego_tinker.open: When I get my workshop, boss, I already know the sign. Two colours, and the letters a little crooked, on purpose.

options.reply: Because perfect is boring, my friend. A crooked sign says a person made it with their hands, and that person will fix your thing properly.
You'll hold the ladder, and I'll hang it, and we'll both get it slightly wrong. Deal, boss, it's a deal.
Yellow and blue, like the kiosk had. Don't laugh, my friend, this is a very serious decision.

esteban_bloodmage.open: Valparaiso is built on hills so steep the city runs old lifts up the slopes, {player}. I rode one to the hospital every morning for nineteen years.

options.reply: Fog on the harbour, the lift creaking, and an old man at the top who sold me coffee and asked who'd been stabbed overnight. He always knew before I did.

options.text: Nineteen years of creaking? Brave man.
options.reply: Braver than you'd think. One of them dropped two metres once with me inside. I filed a complaint, in triplicate.
The hills, yes. The hospital, more than I expected. It held me up in ways I didn't notice until it was gone.

esteban_bloodmage.open: I'm drafting a standard of practice for blood magic, {player}. Eleven clauses so far. I expect nobody to adopt it, and I keep drafting anyway.

options.text: What does the first clause say?
options.reply: That the price is named before the work, to the person who'll pay it, and that their answer binds the practitioner. Everything else follows from that one.

options.text: Why bother, if nobody will use it?
options.reply: Because the lack of it appals me. Someone has to write the first draft, and I'd rather it was a surgeon than a pirate.

esteban_bloodmage.open: My sister Paz is in Santiago, {player}, or was. Her children called me the uncle who explains exactly how bones heal. I'd give a great deal to explain it to them again.

options.text: Have you looked for her on the lists?
options.reply: At every hub I pass. Her name hasn't appeared, and I've learned not to read that as anything at all. Absence of evidence, as we say.

options.text: I'd have liked to hear that lecture.
options.reply: You'd have been bored inside five minutes. They loved it, though, or they were very polite children.

giorgi_primalist.open: You walk too fast for this ground, {player}, slow down, slow down. In Kazbegi I kept sheep for twenty summers, high on the mountain, six months without a road.

options.reply: A dog, a flock, a wooden hut, and me. I spoke to nobody for weeks, and it was normal. Here people worry about me. It is touching and very tiring.

options.text: You're very big for a shepherd.
options.reply: Ha, yes, very big. The wolves agreed, they stayed away. My size was most of my job, my friend.
Every morning I smell the air first. This place is good, the ground tells the truth here. But it is not the same mountain.

giorgi_primalist.open: I want a herd here, {player}. I am serious. The grass above Tarren Mill is as good as anything at home. Nobody takes me seriously, and it makes me angry.

options.reply: Kargi, thank you. This is worth more than you know, from a small mouth to a big man.

options.text: Have you asked the tauren herder?
options.reply: Ha, we argue every week about grazing. He is wrong about almost everything, and I enjoy him very much.

giorgi_primalist.open: My wife is Nino, {player}, a schoolteacher in the village below the pasture. And two daughters, Ana and Mariam. Every autumn I came down to them, and every spring I went back up.

options.reply: Nino thought the mountain was a silliness I would grow out of. Ana is serious like me, Mariam laughs at everything. Her bread, my friend, nobody makes bread like Nino.
I do not know if the village came through. I do not know. But thank you, {player}, for saying it like you believe it.

haruto_runemaster.open: Forgive me, {player}, but your grip is wrong. The thumb sits higher, so. A careless grip makes a careless cut, and a careless cut fails on whoever stands closest.

options.reply: Good, that is the correct question. Again, then, slowly, until the hand remembers without the mind.

options.text: Do you correct everyone you meet?
options.reply: Only the ones worth correcting. You should take it as a compliment, though it rarely feels like one.

options.text: Who taught you to be so exact?
options.reply: A master who corrected me for eleven years before he praised me once. It was a very effective method.

haruto_runemaster.open: There are standing stones in Silverpine South, {player}, with runes nobody can read now. The dark magic from the keep is eating them. I am copying them before they are gone.

options.text: Why copy what nobody can read?
options.reply: Because someone will be able to read them one day, and my copies will be all that is left. Slow work, and unrewarded, and necessary.
It is the only kind I know how to do. Thirty years with a brush teaches you nothing else.

haruto_runemaster.open: I learned runes from a tauren, {player}, an old carver called Hrunn. He had come north out of Thousand Needles, badly hurt. He taught me for one year, and then his wounds took him.

options.reply: From his notes, yes. The result is incomplete in ways I can name, one by one. I think about that every morning.
That is kind, and I hope it is true. He never said so. Teachers rarely do, I am learning.

ivan_warrior.open: Eleven years I drove a tram in Novosibirsk, {player}, Route 13. Four stops in the dark every winter morning, and I loved every one.

options.text: What did you love about it?
options.reply: Everything is on time, everything is in order, and everybody gets home. In this world, nothing is like that.
Not once in eleven years, and I'm very proud of it, like other men are proud of their cars. Now I'm late every day, it's this world.

options.text: And now you swing an axe.
options.reply: Same thing, really, a heavy thing that has to stop exactly where you want. Nobody here knows how to stop.

ivan_warrior.open: The traffic in Orgrimmar, {player}, is the worst I've seen in my life, and I've driven through Novosibirsk in a blizzard. So I started directing it.

options.text: And the orcs listen to you?
options.reply: They do now, yes. The first week they laughed, the second week they stopped, the third week they waited for my hand.
Nobody asks, ever, but somebody has to. Chaos wins if nobody stands in the road.

ivan_warrior.open: Eleven years, {player}, and I never hit anybody, not one person. Children step off the kerb without looking, every day, and I never hit one.

options.reply: Every day, still, here too. With the axe, in a crowd, I think about where everybody is. It's the thing I'm most afraid of.
It's not a record, it's the job. But yes, thank you, I'm proud of it, and I'm afraid of losing it.

leif_primalist.open: You ever have coffee out of a thermos on a stump at five in the morning, {player}? With the fog still sitting in the trees?

options.reply: Quiet, mostly, real quiet. You can hear the woods waking up one bird at a time. Best part of the job, and nobody paid me for it.

options.text: Five in the morning sounds like a punishment.
options.reply: Yep, that's what my ex-wife said. She wasn't wrong, but she missed a good sunrise or two.

options.text: Is that why you're always up before everybody?
options.reply: Pretty much, yep. Twenty-five years of it, and my body doesn't know I quit.

leif_primalist.open: The elves wanted me to cut the old red trees in the Hollow for their roof beams, {player}. First thing anybody here ever asked me for, and I told them no.

options.reply: There was deadwood lying all over the ground, good and dry. You don't cut a living tree that old when it's already given you what you need.
Yep, it is. I've thought about that more than you'd guess. Maybe that's why I said it.
Didn't do it to be good. Just couldn't watch one of those come down for a roof.

leif_primalist.open: My daughter Kaylee fights wildfires back home, {player}, out of Medford. Every time I see smoke out here, I think about her.

options.text: You must be proud of her.
options.reply: Prouder than I've got words for, and I don't have many words to start with. She's braver than I ever was.

options.text: She'll be okay. She sounds tough.
options.reply: Yep, she is. Doesn't stop a dad worrying, though. I just can't call her and check.

liam_suncleric.open: Breathe out loud for me, {player}, good, there you go. It's an old habit. Seventeen years on the fire trucks and ambulances in the Blue Mountains, and I still check everyone's breathing.

options.reply: Both of them, mate. There was no ambulance for an hour either way, so I trained up. At three in the morning nobody cares which badge you're wearing.

options.text: Are my pupils all right too?
options.reply: Ha, they're lovely, mate, equal and reactive. I'll stop now, probably.
I miss the quiet drive home after one that went well. Nothing like it. Here I just walk home, which isn't the same.

liam_suncleric.open: Over at Grom's Rest, {player}, the corruption burns out of people slowly, and nobody had a protocol for it. So I wrote one. Four lines long, wrong in at least one place, and the only one there is.

options.reply: Ha, if I knew that, mate, I'd fix it. That's the fun of being the only one doing it.
Brother and sister, sharp as tacks. Their mum didn't come out of it. I keep an eye on them, that's all, nothing more to it.

liam_suncleric.open: I was married once, {player}, to Jess. She left when I was thirty-seven, because I was never home, and when I was, I never talked. I don't blame her, mate, not for a second.

options.reply: Funny, sharper than me, and far too patient for far too long. She'd be laughing at me now, talking to you like this.
Yeah, I do, don't I? Took losing everything to get there. Bit late for her, but not for everyone.

marco_paladin.open: My shop in Naples had a door that was always open, {player}. Thirty-one years, and I never once locked it in the daytime.

options.text: A locksmith who never locked his door?
options.reply: Ha, you see the joke. A locked door keeps people out, and my work was letting people in. The shop said so before I did.
Once, a boy, sixteen. He came back the next week to return it, because his mother found out who it belonged to. That's the Quartieri.

options.text: It sounds like a good street.
options.reply: The best, and the worst, and the best again. Everybody knew everybody. That's all I want here, a street like that.

marco_paladin.open: The Forsaken have a great many locks, {player}. You'd think the dead would trust each other by now. They trust nobody, and they're right not to.

options.reply: Slowly, one by one. A Forsaken woman brought me a box last month she'd kept shut for twelve years. I opened it and gave it back without looking inside. Now half the passage comes to me.
No, it's the same work. Somebody's locked out of something, and I let them back in. The Light only made it official.

marco_paladin.open: My grandson Matteo was born the February before all this, {player}. I held him four times. I counted, because I'm a man who counts.

options.reply: Maybe so, maybe not. I don't look at the lists, and I'll tell you why one day. Not today, but one day.
Small, loud, and he had my father's chin, poor boy. He held my finger the second time, very hard, like a little vice. That's all I know of him, and I keep it in my pocket with the key.

marcus_stormbringer.open: Did I ever tell you I chased tornadoes as a student, {player}? Across the prairies, in a terrible old Corolla, with no idea what I was doing?

options.reply: Oh, you've done it now. Picture a skinny kid with a clipboard, a paper map, and a car held together with tape, driving toward the thing everyone else is driving away from. Best summers of my life.

options.text: That explains a lot about you.
options.reply: Ha, it does, doesn't it? My mum said the same, and she didn't mean it nicely either.

options.text: Did you ever actually catch one?
options.reply: Twice, and I was too excited to take a single reading either time. Very unprofessional, and I'd do it again tomorrow.

marcus_stormbringer.open: My notes say the coast road's going to get hit hard, {player}, harder than anyone here remembers. I don't know how to tell the orcs without sounding like every stranger who ever lectured them about their own land.

options.text: Show them the data, and let it talk.
options.reply: That's what I'd do at home, and at home it didn't work. But maybe here somebody actually reads it. I'd like to believe that.

options.text: Being right matters more than sounding polite.
options.reply: You're the first person to say that to me in a long time. I've been polite for fifteen years, and polite never saved anyone.

options.text: Maybe they know things you don't, too.
options.reply: They almost certainly do, and I'd love to hear them. That's a good point, and I'm a bit ashamed I didn't make it myself.

marcus_stormbringer.open: My sister Grace has two boys, {player}, Daniel and Joseph. I used to take them storm watching from the car, all three of us with our noses on the glass.

options.text: They sound like they adored you.
options.reply: I hope they did. I was the uncle who explained Rayleigh scattering for twenty minutes, so it's possible they were just being polite. I check the Toronto lists at every hub I pass.

options.text: You'll find them. I believe that.
options.reply: Thank you, I mean it. I'm a forecaster, I deal in probabilities, but I'd like to borrow your certainty for a while.

matias_reaper.open: Ten years I was a bus conductor in Santiago, {player}. Same route, same forty faces every morning. I knew who got off where, and who was having a bad week.

options.reply: Ya, always, I cannot stop. Who will fall, who will steal, who is scared. It is useful here, also.
Very much, yes. People think it is boring, but every morning is a little different. It is like that here too.

options.text: Bet you never missed a stop.
options.reply: Never, not once in ten years. Here I get lost on the first road every time, cachai.

matias_reaper.open: This is a ticket punch, {player}, brass, from the old buses. I click it twice before every fight. Somebody asked if it is for luck. It is not luck.

options.reply: It is how a shift starts. Click, click, and then you work. That is all I will say today.
Gracias, thank you. Most people push. You do not push, and I notice that.

matias_reaper.open: My mother and my brother were in Santiago, {player}. Benjamin, five years younger, he talks too much. I have not found them, on any list.

options.reply: My mother cooks like nobody, and Sunday lunch was for the whole family, football on, Benja talking over the commentator. I miss the noise.
Ya, gracias, thank you. I look at every list. Every one, every hub. Thank you for saying we.

minh_chronomancer.open: For twenty-three years I worked in a dark room in Saigon, {player}, watching a radar scope. Forty aircraft in my head at once, and my job was to choose the future where nobody dies.

options.text: How do you stay that calm?
options.reply: It is not my temperament, it is conditioning. You learn never to let your voice carry what your pulse is doing. Twenty years later, you cannot stop.

options.text: Bet you were great at it.
options.reply: I was good at it, yes, and it cost me a great deal of sleep. Both of those things are true.
Ha, very good. You learn fast, {player}. In another life I would have recruited you.

minh_chronomancer.open: There is a dry riverbed below my ridge in the Barrens, {player}, where time slips. Sometimes water runs from years ago. Sometimes a caravan arrives before it left. Somebody has to watch it.

options.reply: Nobody asked me at all. I appointed myself, because nobody else would. I have made a rota of one, and I am aware of how that sounds.
It is, and almost nobody understands how much. That is exactly why I stay.

minh_chronomancer.open: This tuning fork was my daughter's, {player}, my Linh. She plays the violin, and she was studying music in Melbourne. She gave me her A-note so I would have it with me.

options.reply: Here, listen, until it fades. That is her note. I carry assumptions about where she is, survivable ones, and I have permitted myself those.
Very, much more than her father deserved. I took her to every lesson I could, which was not enough of them.

orlando_witchdoctor.open: Sit, sit, mi amor, I've got a chair for you. Eleven years I was a barber in Santurce, two chairs and a radio, and that shop was the whole neighbourhood.

options.reply: Everything, papi, all of it. Every wedding, every fight, every secret in Santurce. A barber is a priest with better gossip, and I never repeated a word.
Mi amor, I've been dying to ask. Sit still, and we talk the whole time, that's the rule.
Every Saturday, with the radio on and the line out the door. So I make a little shop wherever I stop.

orlando_witchdoctor.open: The trolls at the Shadowpine Altar taught me the spirits, {player}. I treat them like customers. Sit down, tell me what's wrong, I'll fix it, and we talk the whole time.

options.reply: Better than anything, mi amor. A spirit wants to be heard, same as a man in a chair. Everybody wants to be heard.
Ha, nene, not once! But they're loyal, they always come back. Like Don Beni, every Tuesday for nineteen years.

orlando_witchdoctor.open: My whole family was on the island, {player}, all of them. Mami, papi, Yari, the aunts, the cousins. A trader told me once the island came through whole, somewhere across the sea.

options.reply: That's what I believe, mi amor. It's thin, I know, and everybody lets me have it. You let me have it too, thank you.
Mami's arroz con gandules, Papi's bad jokes, and Yari stealing food off my plate every Sunday. Loud, every one of them. I'm the quiet one, if you can believe it.

pavlo_knight.open: I taught history to fourteen-year-olds for sixteen years, {player}. Every spring the same four wars, and every spring a new class who thought it couldn't happen to them.

options.text: And why do you think that is?
options.reply: Ha, you've stolen my line, and I'm delighted. Because it never looks like history while you're inside it. It looks like Tuesday.
Most of them, most years, a little. That's all a teacher gets, and it's more than enough.
Every day, at about nine in the morning, when the first bell would ring. Some days it's worse than others.

pavlo_knight.open: I have six children at the Sepulcher, {player}, twice a week. I teach them whatever I can remember of a world that isn't coming back.

options.reply: Rivers, mostly, and kings, and how ordinary people talk themselves into things. They like the kings best, naturally.
It's a ruined crypt with a draught, but thank you. On a good day it almost feels like one.

pavlo_knight.open: This flask was a gift from my wife, {player}, Oksana, on my first day as a teacher. She was an archivist, and she died when our son was fifteen.

options.reply: She could find anything in any archive in Lviv, and she could never find her keys. She laughed at my jokes, which proves she loved me.
Thank you, it was a long time ago. The tea still tastes better in this flask, and I'm not going to apologise for that.

rhodri_knight.open: Fifteen years in the front row for Pontypridd, {player}, every Saturday, rain or worse. Ask me anything about rugby, go on.

options.text: What's the front row actually for?
options.reply: Standing where the weight comes and not moving, butt. Everyone else gets the glory, we get the cauliflower ears and the pint after. Best job in the world.

options.text: Isn't it just a game for thugs?
options.reply: Oi, oi, I'll forgive you that once, because you've never been in a scrum. It's the most honest game there is, mun, nobody can hide.
The pint after, honest to God. The singing, the lads, the bus home. Not even the game. Saturday, all of it.

rhodri_knight.open: Nobody's ever fallen off anything I built, {player}. Not once, in twenty years of scaffolding. That's the one thing I'm proud of.

options.text: That's something to be proud of.
options.reply: It is, isn't it. You check every tie, every board, every knot, and you never get bored of checking. That's the whole trick.

options.text: Not once? That's a big claim.
options.reply: Not once on Earth, butt. Here's a different story, and I'm not ready to tell it yet. Now in a minute, maybe.

options.text: Is that why you check everyone's straps?
options.reply: Aye, caught me. Can't help it, mun. If it's hanging loose, my hands go to it before my head's decided.

rhodri_knight.open: My sister Carys has two boys, {player}. I used to take them to the match and buy them chips and get told off for it after.

options.reply: Rhys and Owen, eight and six when I last saw them. Proper little terrors, the pair. Rhys wanted to be a hooker, like his uncle, and I nearly cried.

options.text: You'd have been a good dad.
options.reply: Duw, maybe, I don't know. I liked being the uncle, isn't it. All the fun and you hand them back sticky.
Maybe, butt, maybe. I don't say it out loud much in case it hears me. But I'm keeping a chips budget, just in case.

ryan_warlock.open: See this watch, {player}? Bought it with my first bonus in Boston, the day I decided I was the sort of man who wore one.

options.text: And are you? The sort of man?
options.reply: I was, for a long time. Now I wear it so I remember what that man looked like. It keeps perfect time, which is more than he did.
It was obscene, and I earned every cent of it closing down something somebody loved. Good watch, though, I'll give it that.
Ah, you've noticed. Don't worry about that, it's a habit. Mostly when I'm about to say something I shouldn't.

ryan_warlock.open: Every demon I deal with is on a contract I wrote, {player}, clause by clause, pinned up on the wall of my hut. You'd be surprised how honest it keeps them, and me.

options.text: What happens if one breaks the terms?
options.reply: Then I break it back, and it's very sorry. But they rarely try, because I pay exactly on time, every time. Hard to cheat a man who's never late.
Fair, that's fair. Honest's the only trick I've got left, and the contracts are how I keep practising it.

ryan_warlock.open: I've a son, {player}. Conor, he'd be twenty-two now. He came through somewhere on this world, and I haven't put my name on a single list.

options.reply: Because if he's looking, he deserves to find something better than his father. That's the whole reason, and it's a bad one, and I know it.

options.text: He might want to find you anyway.
options.reply: Maybe so, maybe not. I've run that deal a thousand ways, and I can't see the side of it where he gets a good return.

sebastian_bloodmage.open: Twelve years on the grill at my grandmother's place, boss, forty tables and a wood fire. Ask me anything about meat, I dare you.

options.text: How do you know when it's ready?
options.reply: You listen, che. The fat tells you, the smoke tells you, the smell tells you. I could tell a steak was ready from across the room with my back turned.
Get out of my sight, boss. No, come back, I'm joking, sit, I'll make yours medium and you'll thank me for the rest of your life.
Every day, che. The noise, the fire, Saturday night with every table full. Here I cook for whoever turns up, and that's good too, but it's not the same.

sebastian_bloodmage.open: There was a man, boss, Tomas, a sommelier. He left for a job in Mendoza a year before all this. I blame the wine region, personally.

options.text: Do you still think about him?
options.reply: Sometimes, che, sometimes. It doesn't make me sad any more, it's just a good wine you remember. You don't need the bottle to know it was good.
Ha, exactly, boss, exactly, Mendoza's loss! You're a good man, I'm putting extra on your plate tonight.

options.text: A sommelier and a grill man. That's a dangerous pair.
options.reply: Dangerous for everybody's waistline, che. We fed half of Palermo between us, and argued about every bottle.

sebastian_bloodmage.open: The Forsaken barely eat, boss. That was the hardest thing about landing here, and I'm working on a recipe they can actually taste.

options.reply: Close, che, very close. Strong smoke, a lot of salt, something with a bite. The farmer's neighbour tried it last week and almost smiled.

options.text: Why does it matter so much to you?
options.reply: Because an empty table is the worst thing in the world, boss. If I can get one dead man to sit down and enjoy a plate, then nobody's table is empty.

options.text: Make sure I get a taste first.
options.reply: You'll be the first living mouth on it, che, after me. That's a promise.

silas_rogue.open: See this coin, {player}? Two euros, Belgian. It was in my pocket when I landed, and I've flipped it for every choice since.

options.reply: Every one that matters, which is how I make sure none of them do. Pretty clever of me, eh? Don't answer that.

options.text: Flip it now. Heads, you tell me the truth.
options.reply: Ha, nice try. It came up tails, look. Well, it would have, I didn't actually flip it.
Lonely, sure, maybe, about forty percent. The other sixty's very efficient, though.

silas_rogue.open: The port at three in the morning, {player}, all lit up, cranes going, not a soul about. That's the one thing about Antwerp I'll admit to missing.

options.text: What did you do there? The real version.
options.reply: Ah, that's for later, when I know you better. Today's answer is crane driver, and it's very convincing.

options.text: Ratchet must feel like home, then.
options.reply: It's the only shape of place I can read, ports. You know who's lying by how they walk the planks.

silas_rogue.open: The real version, then, since you've earned it. Security guard, {player}, five years watching camera feeds at the port. That's the whole glamorous truth.

options.reply: Because the real one has something in it I don't like. I watched a lot of things on those screens, and I didn't always say what I saw.

options.text: Thank you for the true one.
options.reply: Don't get used to it. Well, maybe get a little used to it, with you. Sixty percent used to it.

sondre_stormbringer.open: I taught sailing on the Hardangerfjord for four summers, to teenagers. Most of what I know about people I learned in a dinghy.

options.reply: That the asking is the part that kills people. You say get down once, clearly, early, and then you trust them to do it. Shouting only frightens them.
Every day, a little. The sea here is the wrong colour, but it moves the same way, and on calm mornings I can almost pretend.

options.text: Teaching teenagers? You're braver than you look.
options.reply: Ha, that is the bravest thing I have ever done, and I have been in a storm I made myself. They are terrifying.

sondre_stormbringer.open: My sister Ingrid is four years younger than me and much braver. My father captains a ferry and my mother is a dentist. They are in Bergen.

options.text: You always talk about them in the present tense.
options.reply: Yes, I do, on purpose, every time. It is like holding a door open with my foot. I am not ready to take my foot away.
Loud, fearless, rude to everyone she loves. She would get on very well with some of you, and she would tease me without mercy.

options.text: Bergen sounds like a good place to be from.
options.reply: It rains nearly every day and nobody minds. That is the best thing I can say about anywhere, I think.

sondre_stormbringer.open: People think I want power, because of what I can do. I do not. I have plenty of power, and that is the whole problem.

options.reply: Control, only that. A whole day without being afraid of my own hands. That is all, and some days it feels like a great deal to ask.

options.text: Practising alone isn't the way, you know.
options.reply: I know, I know. Everyone tells me so, and they are probably right. It is only that alone, the only person I can hurt is me.

options.text: You haven't hurt anyone with us.
options.reply: Not yet, no. Thank you, I think. I will try to hear it as a fact and not as luck.

tomas_warrior.open: I'll get this out of the way early, {player}, because it always comes out as a brag. I arrived forty feet in the air and landed in a tree. Walked away with a scratch.

options.reply: See, I tried to say it humbly, and it still came out like that. I've given up fixing the delivery.

options.text: What were you doing up there?
options.reply: Rigging a concert hall in Prague, four in the morning, up in the grid. Eighteen years of hanging heavy things over people who never looked up.
Afterwards, yeah, properly. During, I was just annoyed I'd dropped my good spanner.

tomas_warrior.open: People here build fast and tie off badly, {player}, and I physically can't walk past it. I fix scaffolding all over Fenris Isle, and they pay me in food and arguments.

options.reply: Because one day it falls on somebody, and I'd know I walked past. I've never been the reason something fell, and I'm keeping that record.

options.text: Sounds like you're the island's rigger now.
options.reply: Ha, nobody hired me, but yeah, I suppose I am. First steady gig I've ever had.

tomas_warrior.open: My parents are in Brno, {player}, or they were. Dad's a welder, Mum's a nurse. I moved to Prague at twenty and only went home at Christmas, which I regret now.

options.reply: Dad taught me knots before I could read, Mum taught me to look up before I walk under anything. Between them they made a rigger.
I hope so. I hope they're together, wherever Brno came down. That's the version I let myself think about.

yiannis_paladin.open: Every soul the sea gives up on this shore, {player}, I am there to pull them out. I was there for the first one, before the elves even had tents.

options.reply: An elf girl, not breathing. I did what we do on the harbour, and while I did it, light came into my hands. She breathed, and I sang her a couplet about it.
Because I was already in the water, re. God does not choose the best man, He chooses the one who is wet already.

options.text: Did you sing for me when I came out?
options.reply: Of course I did, little one, a very good one, about your terrible hair. I will sing it at your wedding.

yiannis_paladin.open: Eleni and the girls, Maria and Katerina, are in Chania. Every night I talk to them on the beach, out loud. I do not care who hears.

options.reply: Everything, my friend. Who came out of the water, what I ate, what foolish thing the young ones did. Tonight I will tell them about you.
The sea carries everything somewhere, re. Maybe not to Chania, but somewhere. That is enough for an old man.
I will, and Eleni will ask if you are eating properly, and I will lie for you.

yiannis_paladin.open: People ask me how I still believe, here, in this strange place. As if the Light in my hands should make me doubt the saint on my wall.

options.reply: No, re, never. A fisherman always knew there was something under the water he could not see. Now I can see a little more of it, that is all.

options.text: Maybe the Light is the saint.
options.reply: Maybe, my friend, maybe. I do not need to know which is which. I just need it to come when the child is not breathing.

options.text: I don't know how you do it.
options.reply: You do not need to know. Sit with me some evening, and watch the sea, and maybe you will feel it a little.

friend.open: I have three sons, {player}. All three went to Bishkek for work. I understood, truly. But six generations ended with them, and I never told them it was all right. I am afraid they think I blamed them.

options.text: If you find them, tell them.
options.reply: Aga, that is the first thing I will say. Then we drink tea. Then I will hold my grandsons and say nothing at all.
Maybe they do. A father hopes. Thank you, {player}, for letting me speak it aloud.

sworn.open: In my family, {player}, you give the route only to someone you trust with your life. I do not have it whole yet. When I do, you will walk it with me.

options.reply: Then it is decided, my friend. Step where I step, and later, I will step where you step.
Ha, good, an old man needs a tea carrier. You are family now, balam.

reconciled.open: {name} and I sat at one fire and talked it through, like elders. We are at peace now, and I wanted you to know.

options.reply: Jakshy, it is good. Tea tastes better after.
I did, of course, the right way. They drank three cups, so I knew it was finished.

friend.open: Okay, a secret, {player}. There was a girl, Elif. My mother had very firm plans for us, and I was getting used to the idea. She laughed at all my jokes, even the bad ones, which was all of them.

options.text: Do you think about her a lot?
options.reply: Some nights, yes. Not like a love song, more like a door I never got to open. I hope she found someone with better jokes.

options.text: Thank you for telling me, Berat.
options.reply: I've never told anybody here, not one person. You're on the short list now, canim, the very short one.

sworn.open: My grandmother used to say you only know who your family is when you're the one who's sick, {player}. I've been sick, a bit, inside, and you stayed with me.

options.reply: Of course, he says, like it's nothing! It's everything, {player}. You're family now, the real kind, no notebook needed.
She'd love you, she'd feed you until you couldn't walk, and then she'd tell the whole street you're a doctor.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} sat down and talked it through, properly, no jokes. We're good again, and I wanted you to hear it first.

options.reply: It is, eh? I hate being on bad terms with anybody, it gives me a toothache in my soul.
Okay, maybe one, at the very end, a small one. But it landed, so it counts as healing.

friend.open: I had a blue heeler back home, {player}, called Biscuit. Went everywhere with me, sat outside the snake house every day. I miss her more than most people, and I'm a bit embarrassed about that.

options.reply: Yeah, you're right. Somebody's looking after her, I reckon, somebody kind. That's the version I keep.
Barked at every snake and never once went near one. Smartest animal I ever met, and I've met heaps.

sworn.open: I've always trusted animals more than people, {player}. You're the first person I'd trust the way I trust a snake I've handled for ten years. That's the biggest compliment I've got, mate.

options.reply: Good, because I don't hand that out, not ever. You're family now.
Don't tell her, but yeah, mate. Even more than the scorpion.

reconciled.open: {name} and I sorted it, properly, and we're good now. Wanted you to hear it from me first.

options.reply: Cheers, mate, I appreciate it. Nobody bit anybody, either.
Me, believe it or not. You learn when to back off from a cornered animal.

friend.open: When I landed in that grass fire, hermano, I wasn't alone. Others came through with me. I was the only one who walked out. I think about them every time I light a camp.

options.reply: Maybe not, hermano. My head knows that, and my heart is slower. Thank you for saying it.

options.text: That's why you go back in.
options.reply: Yes, exactly, every single time. You see me very clearly, hermano.

sworn.open: On the brigade, hermano, you'd follow your partner into any fire, no questions. I'd follow you into any fire. There's nothing bigger I can tell you.

options.reply: Eso, then we're brigade, forever. My mother is going to love you.
Ay, hermano, you sound exactly like her. Okay, okay, for you, I'll try.

reconciled.open: {name} and I talked it out, properly, no shouting, I promise. We're good now, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: Gracias, hermano, really. It feels better, like rain after the dry season.
A little shouting, at the start. Then we laughed. That's how you know it's finished.

friend.open: When the plant shut, {player}, I spent four years on the sofa. Stopped answering the phone. Our Jade came round every Sunday and made me eat. I've never told her what that did for me.

options.text: You'll get the chance to tell her.
options.reply: Hope so, love. First pint I buy her, that's what I'm saying. Then I'll go quiet again, she'll be used to that.
Aye, well, there it is. Seemed like you ought to know why I won't sit still. Don't go spreading it.

sworn.open: On the floor, you didn't say you cared about your crew, {player}. You just never let owt past you to them. You're crew now. That's the most I've got to say.

options.reply: Aye, well, give over before I get something in my eye.
It's meant to. Now let's get a pint before this turns into a speech.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} had it out, properly. We're sorted now, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: Give over, love. But aye, it's good.
I did, obviously. That's how you know it's sorted in Sheffield.

friend.open: Boss, I wanted to say, you're not a customer any more, okay? You're one of my people now, and my people get everything fixed for free.

options.text: Free repairs for life? I'm honoured.
options.reply: For life, my friend, and I mean it. Bring me your broken things and your bad days, both work the same way.

options.text: You're one of mine too, Diego.
options.reply: Ha, okay, now you're going to make me cry on my own boots. Stop it, boss.

sworn.open: I'm going to show you something nobody's seen, boss. Here, this is Senora Chispa. She's the beetle. I want you there when she walks.

options.reply: Good, good, my friend. Then I'll stop being scared of finishing her, because somebody's going to be there.
She is, eh? My mother would've said so too, and then asked why it took me eighteen years.

reconciled.open: So, me and {name}, we talked. Properly, no shouting. I think we're okay now, boss, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: Yeah, it is. People are harder to fix than machines, but they stay fixed longer when you do it right.
Ha, I know, I know, we're both stubborn like old bolts. But we got there, my friend.

friend.open: I owe you an explanation for why I ask everyone, {player}. On a Bloodsail ship I took a prisoner's blood to save their captain, and I didn't ask him. He died that night.

options.reply: Every time, of everyone, on the record. It doesn't balance the account, but it's the only payment I can make.

options.text: Thank you for telling me the truth.
options.reply: You're owed it. I won't ask for your consent to my company without telling you what that company has done.

sworn.open: I've told you I'd let you hold the knife, {player}. Now I'd let you tell me to put it down, and I'd listen. That's a great deal more.

options.text: I'll only ever say it if I mean it.
options.reply: I know you will. That's precisely why I'd listen.

options.text: Then we look after each other.
options.reply: Agreed, with full and informed consent on both sides. It's the best contract I've ever entered.

reconciled.open: {name} and I spoke at length, and frankly. We've resolved it, and I wanted you to know it was resolved properly.

options.reply: As am I. An unresolved conflict festers, and I'd rather not have to treat it later.
Meaning we each named what we'd done, and the other agreed to it. Old habits, I'm afraid.

friend.open: Every autumn, {player}, on the right day, I walk down to the lower ground. I bring the herd down. There is no herd. I tied the bell so it cannot ring. I think I am walking down to nobody.

options.text: Next autumn I'll walk with you.
options.reply: You would do this? Kargi, my friend, kargi. Then I will not walk down to nobody, I will walk down with somebody.

options.text: You're walking down to them, in your heart.
options.reply: Ki, maybe that is it. You put words on it better than I can, my friend.

sworn.open: At a Georgian table, {player}, the last toast is for those who would stand with you on any mountain. I raise it to you, gaumarjos.

options.reply: Kargi, you say it well. You are family now, my friend, and the big man does not say this lightly.
Then we stand together, on every mountain. That is the whole toast.

reconciled.open: {name} and I sat at one table and talked it through, with wine. We are at peace now, and I wanted you to know.

options.reply: Ha, you learn Georgian! Yes, it is good, very good.
Me, of course, I am the tamada always. The toasts made it easier.

friend.open: I have two students, {player}. The elder, Edrin, is better than I was at his age. I have never told him so. My master waited eleven years to praise me, and I have been copying his mistake.

options.reply: You are right, of course. I will, soon. It is the hardest stroke I know.

options.text: He'd be glad to hear it.
options.reply: Perhaps that is exactly why it is difficult. Thank you for listening, {player}.

sworn.open: There was someone, {player}, for twenty years. Kenji, a potter, across the river. We never said it out loud in front of anyone. I am saying it now, to you, because I have decided not to waste any more time.

options.text: Thank you for telling me, Haruto.
options.reply: Thank you for being someone I could tell. That is the whole of it. Let us have tea.
His hands were always grey with clay, and his kiln was always warm. I will tell you the rest slowly, over many mornings.

reconciled.open: {name} and I have spoken, properly, and we are at peace. I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: So am I, and it surprised me. It was a good conversation.
I did, of course, and properly. They noticed, and it helped.

friend.open: Sonya's birthday is the third of March, {player}, and Katya's is the eleventh of August. I've missed three of each now. Every one, I make a cake in my head.

options.text: We'll find them in time for the next one.
options.reply: From your mouth to God's ears, as my mother says. I'll make a real cake, the bad one from the box, they love it.
Medovik, honey cake, ten layers. Natasha makes it, I eat it, this is the system, and it works.

sworn.open: On my route I never had a passenger I'd call family, {player}. You're the first, and that's all I'm going to say about it.

options.text: You're family to me too, Ivan.
options.reply: Good, then you ride for free, forever, front seat. Don't make me say more.

options.text: That's the most you've ever said.
options.reply: And it's the last time, so remember it well. Now we go, we're late.

reconciled.open: Me and {name}, we sorted it, properly, like adults. I wanted to tell you before the gossip gets on the tram.

options.reply: Me too, honestly. Less complaining now, well, a little less.
I did, on time, of course. Somebody has to keep the schedule.

friend.open: I'm going to tell you something, {player}, and I won't tell it twice. My falling partner, Travis. A dead limb came out of a tree I was cutting. That's why I yell about the canopy.

options.reply: That's what everybody said. Took me years to even half believe it. Hearing it from you helps a little.
Yep, I figured it was time. You're the first one out here I've told. Seemed like you ought to know why I'm the way I am.

sworn.open: Up a tree, you only trust one person on the ground to watch the canopy for you, {player}. For a long time nobody. Now it's you.

options.reply: I know you will. That's why I can climb again.

options.text: Then climb, Leif. I've got you.
options.reply: Yep, you always do. Alright, I'm going up.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} hashed it out. Took a while, both of us being stubborn as old growth, but we're good now.

options.reply: Yep, me too. Feels lighter, carrying it around without that.
Old trees grow slow, {player}. We got there.

friend.open: The summer of 2019, {player}, the fires came through the mountains. Weeks on the line. I lost two of my crew and half my street, and I went straight back to work. That's when the sleeping stopped.

options.reply: No, mate, I didn't. There was always another call. Nobody else has heard me admit that.

options.text: That's why you go in alone.
options.reply: Yeah, I reckon it is. If I go in alone, nobody else gets hurt. Except it doesn't work like that, does it?

sworn.open: On a crew, {player}, you trust your partner with the other end of the stretcher. I'd trust you with the other end of anything. I can't say it any bigger than that, mate.

options.reply: Good on ya. Then we're crew, permanent. I'll put the kettle on.
Ha, I might, now. Funny how that works when you've got somebody watching your back.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} sat down and sorted it, like grown-ups. All square, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: Cheers, mate, appreciate it. Felt good to clear the air.

options.text: Did you make them breathe out loud?
options.reply: Ha, I did, actually. Works on everyone, that.

friend.open: I've never once looked at the lists, {player}, not in three whole years. While I don't look, they're all alive. I wanted to say that out loud to somebody, once.

options.text: When you're ready, I'll come with you to read them.
options.reply: You'd do that, for an old man? Allora, maybe I'll be ready sooner than I thought.

options.text: That's a heavy thing to carry alone.
options.reply: It is, and I'm tired of carrying it. Now you've got a corner of it, and that's lighter already.

sworn.open: In my quarter, a person you'd trust with your door was family, {player}. You are family to me now, and that's not something I say to anyone.

options.text: Then you're family to me too, Marco.
options.reply: Good, it's settled. And family doesn't pay for drinks when I'm at the table, so put that away.
Don't be honoured, be family. It's more work, and it's better.

reconciled.open: {name} and I spoke, properly, like people of sense. It's mended now, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: So am I. A crack in a street spreads if nobody fixes it.
Ha, an old man never tells that. But I paid for the drinks, so you can guess.

friend.open: There's something I've never told anybody here, {player}. A flood once took a trailer park my warning had named. People died who didn't need to. That's why I say everything three times.

options.text: You warned them. That's on the people who ignored it.
options.reply: That's what I tell myself at three in the morning. Hearing somebody else say it is different, and I'm grateful.

options.text: Thank you for trusting me with that.
options.reply: You're one of the very few, you know. Probably the only one on this whole world.

sworn.open: My mum told me every Christmas that my job was a waste of a good degree, {player}. The last Christmas, she said it too. I've wanted to tell somebody that for a very long time.

options.reply: I think she might have been, yes. It's strange, hearing myself agree with you on that.

options.text: I'd have loved to meet her anyway.
options.reply: Ha, she'd have liked you. She'd have told you to get a proper job, but she'd have liked you.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} talked it through, properly. Two very stubborn weather systems, but they've merged now, and we're okay. I wanted you to know.

options.reply: It is, isn't it? Clear skies, for once, and I didn't even have to forecast it.
It did, sorry, slow-moving fronts. But we got there in the end.

friend.open: The punch was my father's, {player}. We fought when I was twenty-four, and we did not speak for two years. Then he died, and I found out on the phone after a shift. I am learning to write here so I can write him a letter.

options.text: When it's done, I'll read it.
options.reply: Gracias, I mean it. I need someone to tell me it makes sense. There is nowhere to send it, but I want to write it anyway.

options.text: He knew you didn't hate him.
options.reply: I hope so, every day I hope. Thank you for saying it, {player}. I needed somebody to say it.

sworn.open: On the bus I watched everybody, {player}, but nobody watched me. You watch me. You wait for my words. You are family, weon, that is all I have to say.

options.reply: Ya, good, then it is decided. Now do not make me cry at the front.

options.text: Take all the time you need.
options.reply: That is exactly why, cachai. Thank you, always.

reconciled.open: {name} and I talked, properly, all of it. We are okay now, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: Ya, it is good. Less silence now.
Me, believe it or not. I am learning.

friend.open: When it happened, {player}, I was in the middle of a handover. I had just said you have control. Forty aircraft, handed to a colleague, and then I vanished. I will never know what happened next.

options.text: You did your job right to the end.
options.reply: I did my job, yes. I keep telling myself that, and today, hearing you say it, I almost believe it.

options.text: That's what keeps you on watch.
options.reply: Yes, exactly that. If I stop watching, something might go wrong that I could have stopped. You understand me very well.

sworn.open: I have trusted very few people with the watch, {player}, in two worlds. You have it now, whenever you want it. You have control.

options.reply: Copy that, you have it. Then I am going to sleep, properly, for the first time in twenty years.
A shared watch, then. That is better than any rota I ever made.

reconciled.open: {name} and I have reviewed the whole sequence together, properly. We are clear now, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: So am I, very much. It landed safely.

options.text: Did you write an incident report?
options.reply: A short one, yes. They laughed at it, which helped.

friend.open: There was somebody, {player}, back home. Gabriel, a nurse. A year together, and it was going well. He'd started leaving a toothbrush at my place. I think about that toothbrush more than I should.

options.reply: Calm, the opposite of me, and he laughed at all my jokes, even the bad ones. Especially the bad ones, mi amor.
Gracias for listening, papi. I listen to everybody, and nobody listens to me, except you.

sworn.open: In my shop, {player}, family wasn't only blood. It was whoever kept coming back to sit in the chair. You're family now, mi amor, forever.

options.reply: Wepa, then it's decided. Free haircuts for life, and I'm not joking.
That's exactly it, papi. That's what family means. Ay, now my eyes are wet.

reconciled.open: {name} and I sat down and talked it all out, every word. All fixed now, and I wanted you to hear it from me.

options.reply: Gracias, mi amor. I even cut their hair after, so you know it's real.
Me, obviously, mi amor. But I listened too, I promise.

friend.open: I have a son, {player}, Andriy, twenty-six now. He was studying engineering in Krakow when it happened. We argued about history at dinner every night, and I'd give anything for one more argument.

options.reply: Thank you, I'd like that very much. I check every list, and I haven't found him, but I haven't stopped.
Everything, the Cossacks mostly. He was wrong about all of it, and he was so good at being wrong.

sworn.open: I've stood in front of a great many people, {player}, children and strangers and fools. You're the first in a long while I'd choose to stand in front of. That's my whole speech.

options.reply: Then we'll hold the road together, as long as it needs holding. Have some tea.
It's the shortest I've ever given, and the only one I meant every word of.

reconciled.open: {name} and I have gone over it together, in order, from the beginning. We're at peace now, and I wanted you to know.

options.reply: Thank you, though they did most of the hard work. I mostly poured the tea.

options.text: Did you draw a map of it?
options.reply: A small one, in the dirt, yes. They thought it was very funny, and it helped.

friend.open: You're one of my boys now, {player}, my front row. That means I'll stand in front of anything for you, no questions.

options.text: Then I'll be right behind you.
options.reply: That's the way, butt. You push, I hold, and nothing gets through us.

options.text: Do I have to learn the songs?
options.reply: Every word, mun, and I'll be testing you in the next tavern.

sworn.open: Here, take this. My podger spanner, from the scaffolds at home. Had it on my wrist the day I came through. I want you to have it.

options.reply: You can, and you will, butt. I've got the fire now, I don't need the spanner to hold things together any more.
I know you will. Check your straps with it, now and then, for me.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} had it out, {player}, properly, over a cuppa. I think we're sorted now, and I wanted you to know first.

options.reply: Too short for grudges, aye. Long enough for tea, though.
Nothing much, butt. We both said sorry at the same time and then laughed like idiots.

friend.open: My grandmother raised me in Cork, {player}, a woman called Nora. The rosary and very strong opinions about right and wrong. I'm glad she didn't live to see Boston, and I've never said her name out loud here.

options.text: She'd see who you are now, too.
options.reply: She would, and she'd still have a word or two to say. But maybe she'd say them more quietly, and that's something.

options.text: Thank you for telling me about her.
options.reply: She'd have taken to you. She liked anyone who'd look you in the eye and tell you the truth, God help them.

sworn.open: I said once I'd sign anything you put in front of me without reading it, {player}. It was a joke at the time. It isn't any more.

options.text: I'd never put anything in front of you I wouldn't sign myself.
options.reply: I know you wouldn't. That's why it's the most dangerous thing I've ever meant.

options.text: Then don't read it. I've got you.
options.reply: Grand, then, I won't. No small print, for the first time in my life.

reconciled.open: {name} and I sorted it, properly, no small print. I wanted you to hear it from me before you heard it from the rumour mill.

options.reply: Ah, a gentleman never says. But I bought the round, so draw your own conclusions.
So am I, which surprises me more than anyone. Fair terms all round.

friend.open: Boss, you've got a chair at my table now. Not a guest chair, a family chair. That means you never pay and you never leave hungry.

options.reply: Good, che, because it wasn't really a question. Sit, sit, the meat's nearly ready.

options.text: Do I get to sit next to you?
options.reply: Next to me? Boss, I don't sit. But you get the chair beside where I'd sit, and that's the best one.

sworn.open: Here, boss, take this. My grandmother's chimichurri, the card, in her handwriting. I want somebody else to know it, in case.

options.text: I'll keep it safe. And I'll learn it.
options.reply: Learn it properly, che, the garlic fine, never in a machine. Then one day you cook it for me, and I sit down.
In case I forget how it tasted, boss. That's my real fear, more than dying. Now two of us will remember.

reconciled.open: Me and {name}, we sat down together, boss. Ate, talked, no shouting. I think we're good now, and I wanted you to know.

options.reply: Almost everything, che. Food and time and somebody willing to pass the bread first.

options.text: I'm glad. You both needed it.
options.reply: We did, boss. Life's too short to eat angry.

friend.open: I've a brother, {player}, called Jens. He went to prison for two years over the dock money. I saw it coming on the cameras for months and said nothing, not even to him.

options.text: You could still tell him that.
options.reply: Maybe I could. If I ever find him, that's the first thing he gets. Then a beer. Then probably a punch, from him, and fair enough.

options.text: That's why you step in now.
options.reply: Clever, you, too clever, and yes. Every time I step in, it's the screen I'm stepping into.

sworn.open: I put the coin away for good, {player}. You're the one decision I made without flipping it, and I'm not going to start now.

options.reply: Sixty percent sure. No, that's a lie, a hundred. First hundred of my life.
I'll keep it for luck, then, but I'm never flipping it again. Not for anything that matters.

reconciled.open: Me and {name} squared it, properly, no angles. Wanted you to hear it from me before the rumour mill gets it wrong.

options.text: Good. Did you flip for who went first?
options.reply: Ha, no, I went first, no coin. Growth, they call it, and it's very uncomfortable.
So am I, which surprised me more than anybody. Clean manifest, for once.

friend.open: I would like you to stand beside me when the weather turns, from now on, not behind. I do not ask that of many people.

options.reply: Thank you, truly. Then I will try very hard to be worth standing beside.

options.text: Are you sure? I've seen what you can do.
options.reply: That is exactly why I am asking you, and not someone who has not seen it.

sworn.open: This is my shackle key, from the boats at home. I have worn it every day for six years now. I would like you to hold it for a while.

options.reply: I know you will. That is why it is you, and not anyone else.
Because when I hold it I am afraid, and I want to try being without it, near someone I trust.

reconciled.open: {name} and I talked, properly, without anyone shouting. I think we are all right now, and I wanted you to hear it from me first.

options.reply: So am I. It is easier to stand near someone when you are not at odds with them.
Nothing very much, I think. We were both a little wrong and a little stubborn, and we got tired of it.
